Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Protesters draped themselves in the colorful flag of Tibet and shouted slogans at the Chinese embassy in London on Saturday at the start of a demonstration to mark the 50th anniversary since the Tibetan uprising against China. Protesters have gathered in London to mark the 50th anniversary of the Tibet uprising. "Tibetans in Tibet -- we are with you!" they shouted. "China, China, China -- out, out, out!" The small but fervent group marched from the embassy through west London to Trafalgar Square, where they were due to hear a speech by Thomas Shao Jiang, a Chinese dissident who was one of the student organizers of the Tiananmen Square protest in Beijing in 1989. "I think it's important that Tibet is kept in the world's eye," protester Chris Last told CNN amid placards declaring "50 years too long" and "We are Tibetans, not Chinese." While Tibet is technically autonomous from the central Chinese government, its current government is directed from Beijing. The Dalai Lama, traditionally the spiritual and political leader of the Tibetan Buddhists, lives in exile in India. Tuesday marks the 50th anniversary of a failed 1959 uprising against Beijing's rule that sent the Dalai Lama into exile. Protest organizers said the march was meant to draw public attention to what they say is a deepening crisis a year after China cracked down on protests across Tibet. "(British Prime Minister) Gordon Brown and other world leaders must respond urgently and publicly to the Tibet crisis by taking immediate action," said Stephanie Brigden, director of Free Tibet. "They should demand that China calls off its security stranglehold in Tibet as an essential first step towards backing the Dalai Lama's initiative in finding a long-term and negotiated settlement to China's occupation." Tibetan Buddhists say they resent the slow erosion of their culture amid an influx of Han Chinese, the largest ethnic group in China. That resentment spilled over last March, when Buddhist monks initiated peaceful anti-Chinese protests in the regional capital, Lhasa, on the 49th anniversary of the uprising. The protests soon turned violent, with demonstrators burning vehicles and shops. Some protesters advocated independence from China, while others demonstrated against the growing influence of the Han Chinese in the area and other regions of China with ethnic Tibetan populations. The subsequent crackdown left 18 civilians and one police officer dead, according to the Chinese government. Tibet's self-proclaimed government-in-exile put the death toll from the protests at 140. China accuses the Dalai Lama of fomenting the discord in his homeland -- a charge he denies. "The Dalai Lama demanded the establishment of the so-called 'Greater Tibetan area' on a quarter of the Chinese territory, to drive away Chinese army stationed there guarding the Chinese territory, and to drive away Chinese people of other ethnic groups who lived there for generations. Is such a person a religious figure?" Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi said Saturday. "The conflict between him and us is not religious conflict, human rights conflict, ethnic conflict, nor cultural conflict," Yang said. "The conflict is whether or not to maintain China's unification, and whether or not to permit Tibet to be separated from the Chinese territory." The Dalai Lama has said he does not advocate violence or a separate and independent Tibet. He has said he wants a genuine autonomy that preserves the cultural heritage of the region. "I'm just disgusted with the way the Chinese behave towards the Tibetans. Even if you accept that Tibet has been swallowed up by China, why can't they give to them autonomy, respect their religion, their culture?" protester Bob Hunt said Saturday. "These are peaceable people, one of the most peaceable people in the world." Protester Shobha Trivedi said she hoped the protest march would make people more aware of the situation inside Tibet. "I feel as a human being, what (the) Chinese are doing for 50 years, nobody's bothering with it," she said. "And it's a real shame on everyone."

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Draped in the colorful flag of Tibet, protesters gathered outside the Chinese Embassy in London on Saturday, chanting slogans at the start of a demonstration marking the 50th anniversary of the Tibetan uprising against China.

Protesters assembled in London to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Tibet uprising.

“Tibetans in Tibet -- we are with you!” they shouted. “China, China, China -- out, out, out!”

The small but fervent group marched from the embassy through west London to Trafalgar Square, where they were scheduled to hear a speech by Thomas Shao Jiang, a Chinese dissident who was among the student organizers of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protest in Beijing.

“I think it’s important that Tibet is kept in the world’s eye,” protester Chris Last told CNN, speaking amid placards reading “50 years too long” and “We are Tibetans, not Chinese.”

Although Tibet is technically autonomous from China’s central government, its current government is directed from Beijing. The Dalai Lama, traditionally the spiritual and political leader of Tibetan Buddhists, lives in exile in India.

Tuesday marks the 50th anniversary of the failed 1959 uprising against Beijing’s rule, which forced the Dalai Lama into exile.

Protest organizers said the march was intended to draw public attention to what they describe as a deepening crisis, one year after China cracked down on protests across Tibet.

“(British Prime Minister) Gordon Brown and other world leaders must respond urgently and publicly to the Tibet crisis by taking immediate action,” said Stephanie Brigden, director of Free Tibet. “They should demand that China calls off its security stranglehold in Tibet as an essential first step towards backing the Dalai Lama’s initiative in finding a long-term and negotiated settlement to China’s occupation.”

Tibetan Buddhists say they resent the gradual erosion of their culture amid an influx of Han Chinese, China’s largest ethnic group.

That resentment erupted last March, when Buddhist monks began peaceful anti-Chinese protests in the regional capital, Lhasa, on the 49th anniversary of the uprising. The demonstrations soon turned violent, with protesters setting fire to vehicles and shops.

Some protesters called for independence from China, while others demonstrated against the growing influence of Han Chinese in the area and in other regions of China with ethnic Tibetan populations.

The ensuing crackdown left 18 civilians and one police officer dead, according to the Chinese government. Tibet’s self-proclaimed government-in-exile put the death toll from the protests at 140.

China accuses the Dalai Lama of fomenting discord in his homeland -- an allegation he denies.

“The Dalai Lama demanded the establishment of the so-called ‘Greater Tibetan area’ on a quarter of the Chinese territory, to drive away Chinese army stationed there guarding the Chinese territory, and to drive away Chinese people of other ethnic groups who lived there for generations. Is such a person a religious figure?” Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi said Saturday.

“The conflict between him and us is not religious conflict, human rights conflict, ethnic conflict, nor cultural conflict,” Yang said. “The conflict is whether or not to maintain China’s unification, and whether or not to permit Tibet to be separated from the Chinese territory.”

The Dalai Lama has said he does not advocate violence or a separate, independent Tibet. He has said he seeks genuine autonomy that preserves the region’s cultural heritage.

“I’m just disgusted with the way the Chinese behave towards the Tibetans. Even if you accept that Tibet has been swallowed up by China, why can’t they give to them autonomy, respect their religion, their culture?” protester Bob Hunt said Saturday. “These are peaceable people, one of the most peaceable people in the world.”

Protester Shobha Trivedi said she hoped the march would raise greater awareness of the situation inside Tibet.

“I feel as a human being, what (the) Chinese are doing for 50 years, nobody’s bothering with it,” she said. “And it’s a real shame on everyone.”

Tuesday marks five decades since the unsuccessful 1959 revolt against Beijing’s rule, an uprising that led to the Dalai Lama’s flight into exile.

Organizers of the London march said their goal was to focus public attention on what they describe as a worsening crisis, one year after Chinese authorities suppressed protests throughout Tibet.

“(British Prime Minister) Gordon Brown and other world leaders must respond urgently and publicly to the Tibet crisis by taking immediate action,” said Stephanie Brigden, director of Free Tibet. “They should demand that China calls off its security stranglehold in Tibet as an essential first step towards backing the Dalai Lama’s initiative in finding a long-term and negotiated settlement to China’s occupation.”

Tibetan Buddhists say they are angered by what they see as the gradual weakening of their culture, particularly as more Han Chinese — China’s largest ethnic group — move into the region.

Those tensions erupted last March, when Buddhist monks began peaceful anti-Chinese demonstrations in Lhasa, Tibet’s regional capital, on the 49th anniversary of the uprising. The demonstrations later became violent, with protesters setting fire to vehicles and businesses.

Some participants called for Tibet to become independent from China, while others protested the expanding presence and influence of Han Chinese in Tibet and in other Chinese areas where ethnic Tibetans live.

According to the Chinese government, the crackdown that followed resulted in the deaths of 18 civilians and one police officer. Tibet’s self-declared government-in-exile said 140 people died in the unrest.

Beijing has accused the Dalai Lama of encouraging instability in Tibet, an allegation he rejects.

“The Dalai Lama demanded the establishment of the so-called ‘Greater Tibetan area’ on a quarter of the Chinese territory, to drive away Chinese army stationed there guarding the Chinese territory, and to drive away Chinese people of other ethnic groups who lived there for generations. Is such a person a religious figure?” Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi said Saturday.

“The conflict between him and us is not religious conflict, human rights conflict, ethnic conflict, nor cultural conflict,” Yang said. “The conflict is whether or not to maintain China’s unification, and whether or not to permit Tibet to be separated from the Chinese territory.”

The Dalai Lama has stated that he does not support violence and is not seeking a separate, independent Tibet. He has said his aim is meaningful autonomy that protects the region’s cultural heritage.

“I’m just disgusted with the way the Chinese behave towards the Tibetans,” protester Bob Hunt said Saturday. “Even if you accept that Tibet has been swallowed up by China, why can’t they give to them autonomy, respect their religion, their culture? These are peaceable people, one of the most peaceable people in the world.”

Another protester, Shobha Trivedi, said she hoped the march would help raise awareness about conditions inside Tibet.

“I feel as a human being, what (the) Chinese are doing for 50 years, nobody’s bothering with it,” she said. “And it’s a real shame on everyone.”

counterfactuals.output:
**Pro-Tibet demonstrators mark uprising anniversary outside Chinese Embassy in London**

**LONDON** — Protesters gathered outside the Chinese Embassy in London on Tuesday to mark the 50th anniversary of the 1959 Tibetan uprising, waving Tibetan flags, chanting “Free Tibet” and calling on Beijing to end what they described as decades of political and religious repression in the Himalayan region.

The demonstration, one of several held around the world, commemorated the March 10, 1959, revolt in Lhasa, Tibet’s capital, when thousands of Tibetans surrounded the palace of their spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, amid fears he would be detained by Chinese authorities. The uprising was crushed by Chinese troops, and the Dalai Lama fled across the Himalayas into exile in India, where he has lived ever since.

Outside the embassy in west London, demonstrators held banners reading “Human Rights for Tibet” and “China: Talk to the Dalai Lama.” Some protesters carried photographs of monks and nuns they said had been imprisoned for political or religious activity.

“We are here because Tibetans inside Tibet cannot speak freely,” one protester said during the rally. “Fifty years later, people are still asking for basic rights — the right to practice their religion, preserve their language and live without fear.”

Another demonstrator said the anniversary was not only a remembrance of 1959 but also of more recent unrest. “Last year showed the world that Tibet is not resolved,” the protester said, referring to widespread protests across Tibetan areas in 2008 and the security crackdown that followed.

Tibet has been under Chinese control since the early 1950s, after the People’s Liberation Army entered the region. Beijing says Tibet has been part of China for centuries and argues that its rule ended feudal oppression, brought economic development, built infrastructure and improved living standards.

Many Tibetans in exile and human rights groups dispute that account, saying Chinese policies have restricted religious practice, undermined Tibetan culture and encouraged large-scale migration that has changed the region’s demographics.

The Dalai Lama, now based in Dharamsala, India, has long said he is not seeking independence from China but “genuine autonomy” for Tibetans within the People’s Republic of China. Beijing rejects that position, accusing him of pursuing separatism under another name.

In a statement marking the anniversary, the Dalai Lama said Tibetans had endured “untold suffering” over five decades and called again for dialogue with Chinese leaders. He has repeatedly urged his supporters to remain nonviolent.

China has consistently defended its policies in Tibet. Chinese officials say the region enjoys religious freedom and rapid economic growth, and they blame unrest on what they describe as separatist forces linked to the Dalai Lama.

A Chinese government spokesman has previously said Tibet’s development under Chinese rule is “a fact that cannot be denied,” and that Beijing opposes any attempt to “split China.” Officials have also said the Dalai Lama must abandon separatist aims before meaningful talks can resume.

British officials have called for restraint and dialogue. The UK government has said it recognizes Tibet as part of China, while also raising concerns about human rights and urging Chinese authorities to engage with representatives of the Dalai Lama.

The London protest remained largely peaceful, with police stationed outside the embassy as demonstrators marched, prayed and observed moments of silence for those killed or imprisoned over the past five decades.

For many at the rally, the anniversary was both a solemn commemoration and a call for renewed international attention.

“Fifty years is too long,” a protester said. “We want governments to remember Tibet not just today, but until there is justice.”

The demonstration, organised by pro-Tibet campaign groups and members of the Tibetan community in Britain, began with protesters gathering near the Chinese embassy before making their way through the capital toward Trafalgar Square. Many carried Tibetan flags and placards bearing slogans such as “Free Tibet,” “China Out of Tibet,” “Long Live the Dalai Lama,” and “Human Rights for Tibet.”

At Trafalgar Square, speakers addressed the crowd from the steps below Nelson’s Column, calling for the release of political prisoners and an end to what they described as Chinese repression in Tibet. Protesters also chanted appeals to Prime Minister Gordon Brown, urging him to raise Tibet directly with Chinese leaders and to support international scrutiny of China’s policies in the region.

The annual march commemorates the Tibetan uprising of March 10, 1959, when Tibetans in Lhasa rose up against Chinese rule. The revolt was suppressed by Chinese forces, and the Dalai Lama, Tibet’s spiritual leader, fled into exile in India, where he has remained since.

This year’s protest carried added resonance because of the continuing fallout from the 2008 unrest in Tibet and Tibetan-populated areas of China. Demonstrations that began in Lhasa in March 2008, ahead of the Beijing Olympics, spread to other regions and were followed by a major Chinese security crackdown. Human rights groups accused Chinese authorities of using excessive force, imposing tight controls on monasteries and restricting access for foreign journalists and observers. Beijing said the measures were necessary to restore order and blamed violent rioters for attacks on civilians and property.

Several demonstrators in London said the 2008 crackdown showed that international attention had not produced meaningful change for Tibetans. “We are here because people inside Tibet cannot speak freely,” one protester said. “The world must not forget them.”

China rejects accusations that it oppresses Tibetans, saying Tibet has benefited from economic development, infrastructure investment and improved living standards since what Beijing calls the region’s “peaceful liberation” in 1951. Chinese officials maintain that Tibet is an inseparable part of China and accuse the Dalai Lama of seeking to split the country, despite his repeated statements that he supports genuine autonomy for Tibet rather than independence.

Beijing has long described the Dalai Lama as a political separatist operating under the cover of religion. It strongly objects to foreign leaders meeting him, arguing that such contacts interfere in China’s internal affairs. Supporters of the Dalai Lama say he is a Nobel Peace Prize laureate and a religious leader whose calls for non-violence and dialogue should be recognised.

The British government has in the past said it recognises Tibet as part of the People’s Republic of China while urging dialogue between Beijing and representatives of the Dalai Lama. Protesters on Tuesday said that position was not enough, calling on Brown’s government to press China publicly over human rights and access to Tibet.

As the march reached Trafalgar Square, demonstrators held a moment of silence for Tibetans they said had died under Chinese rule. Monks in maroon robes led prayers, while campaigners distributed leaflets about political prisoners and restrictions on religious practice.

Police monitored the protest, which appeared peaceful. Organisers said the march was intended not only as a commemoration of the 1959 uprising but also as a reminder that the Tibet issue remained unresolved more than half a century later.

“The message today is simple,” one speaker told the crowd. “Tibetans must be allowed to live with dignity, preserve their culture and practise their religion freely.”

**Tibet supporters protest in London as China defends its rule**

**LONDON, March 10 —** Hundreds of demonstrators gathered in central London on Sunday to protest against Chinese rule in Tibet, waving Tibetan flags, chanting slogans and calling for greater international pressure on Beijing over human rights and religious freedoms in the Himalayan region.

The protest, held to mark the anniversary of the 1959 Tibetan uprising against Chinese rule, drew Tibetan exiles, rights activists and supporters who marched near Chinese diplomatic offices under a heavy police presence. Some carried placards reading “Free Tibet” and “Human Rights for Tibet,” while others displayed images of the Dalai Lama, Tibet’s exiled spiritual leader.

“We are here because Tibetans inside Tibet cannot speak freely,” said Tenzin Dorjee, a London-based Tibetan activist. “They face restrictions on religion, language and movement. The international community should not look away.”

Another demonstrator, Sarah Collins, who said she had joined Tibet-related protests for more than a decade, said the issue was not only about independence. “It is about basic rights — the right to worship, the right to preserve a culture, the right not to be punished for peaceful expression,” she said.

China rejects accusations that it represses Tibetans and says its rule has brought development, infrastructure and improved living standards to what it calls the Tibet Autonomous Region. Beijing says Tibet has been part of China for centuries and denounces pro-Tibet independence activism as a threat to national sovereignty.

Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiechi has previously defended Beijing’s position, saying China’s policy in Tibet is an internal matter and accusing the Dalai Lama and his supporters of pursuing separatism. “The Dalai Lama is not a purely religious figure, but a political exile engaged in activities aimed at splitting China,” Yang said in remarks reflecting Beijing’s long-standing view.

Tibet’s political status has been a source of dispute for decades. Chinese forces entered Tibet in 1950, and Beijing later asserted control through an agreement it says confirmed Chinese sovereignty. Tibetans who oppose Chinese rule say the agreement was imposed under pressure and that Tibet had functioned with substantial independence before China’s takeover.

The Dalai Lama fled Tibet in 1959 after a failed uprising against Chinese rule and established a government-in-exile in Dharamshala, India. He has since become a global advocate for Tibetan culture, religious freedom and non-violence. In recent decades, he has said he seeks genuine autonomy for Tibet within China rather than outright independence, a position known as the “Middle Way.” Beijing remains deeply suspicious of him and refuses to engage unless he accepts Tibet and Taiwan as inseparable parts of China.

At the London protest, organizers called on the British government to raise Tibet in meetings with Chinese officials and to press for access to Tibetan areas for journalists, diplomats and independent observers.

“China says Tibetans are happy, but then it blocks the world from seeing what is happening there,” said Maya Shah, a campaigner with a Tibet advocacy group. “If there is nothing to hide, allow independent monitors in.”

The Chinese Embassy in London has in past statements described such protests as anti-China activities that misrepresent conditions in Tibet. Chinese officials say Tibetans enjoy religious freedom and cultural protections, and that economic investment has improved education, health care and transport links across the region.

The protest ended peacefully, with demonstrators singing the Tibetan national anthem and observing a moment of silence for Tibetans who activists say have died in custody, in protests or through self-immolation. Police reported no major incidents.

**Tibetans Mark 50th Anniversary of Uprising With London Protests as China Renews Accusations Against Dalai Lama**

**LONDON —** Tibetans and human rights campaigners gathered in London to mark the 50th anniversary of the 1959 Tibetan uprising, using the occasion to call for renewed international pressure on China over its rule in Tibet and to demand accountability for the violence that erupted in Lhasa and other Tibetan areas in 2008.

Demonstrators assembled outside Chinese diplomatic buildings and in central London, carrying Tibetan flags, placards and portraits of the Dalai Lama. Many chanted slogans calling for freedom in Tibet, the release of political prisoners and an end to what campaigners describe as decades of repression under Chinese rule.

The anniversary commemorates the March 10, 1959 uprising in Lhasa, when Tibetans rose against Chinese control amid fears for the safety of the Dalai Lama. The rebellion was crushed by Chinese forces, and the Dalai Lama fled across the Himalayas into exile in India, where he has lived ever since. Beijing says Tibet has been an inseparable part of China for centuries and describes its rule as having brought development, modernization and the end of feudal oppression.

In London, the campaign group Free Tibet said the anniversary should not be treated only as a historical milestone, but as a moment for governments to confront what it called ongoing abuses. The group urged Britain and other countries to press Beijing to end political repression in Tibet, allow independent observers and journalists access to Tibetan areas, release those detained for peaceful protest, and engage in meaningful dialogue with Tibetan representatives.

Campaigners also called attention to the unrest that swept Lhasa in March 2008, ahead of the Beijing Olympics. What began as peaceful demonstrations by monks marking the anniversary of the 1959 uprising escalated into the most serious disturbances in Tibet in decades. Protests spread from Lhasa to other Tibetan-populated regions in western China, including parts of Sichuan, Gansu and Qinghai provinces.

The 2008 unrest remains deeply disputed. Chinese authorities said rioters in Lhasa attacked civilians, burned shops and vehicles, and killed 18 civilians and a police officer, later putting the total number of deaths at more than 20. Beijing portrayed the violence as a criminal outbreak of separatist disorder and said security forces acted with restraint.

Tibetan exile groups and human rights organizations gave far higher estimates, saying that scores — and in some accounts more than 200 — Tibetans were killed in the subsequent crackdown across Tibetan areas. They accused Chinese security forces of using excessive force, carrying out mass arrests and imposing sweeping restrictions on monasteries and communities. Because access to the region was heavily restricted, the competing death tolls have never been independently verified.

China has repeatedly accused the Dalai Lama and his supporters of fomenting unrest, alleging that what it calls the “Dalai clique” organized or encouraged the 2008 protests as part of a campaign to split Tibet from China. Chinese officials have also accused exile groups of exploiting international sympathy and using the anniversary of the uprising to undermine Chinese sovereignty.

The Dalai Lama has rejected those accusations, saying he does not seek Tibetan independence but “genuine autonomy” within the People’s Republic of China. He has consistently denied involvement in organizing violence and has said Tibetan grievances stem from restrictions on religion, culture, language and political expression. His envoys held intermittent talks with Chinese officials in the 2000s, but those discussions produced no breakthrough and have since stalled.

The anniversary has sharpened the divide between Beijing’s narrative and that of Tibetans in exile. For China, March 10 is linked to what it views as a failed rebellion by an old ruling elite and separatist forces. For many Tibetans, it is a national day of mourning and resistance, symbolizing the loss of political freedom and the beginning of the Dalai Lama’s exile.

In London, speakers at the demonstrations said the events of 2008 showed that Tibetan anger had not faded after half a century. Activists argued that China’s heavy security presence in Tibet, restrictions on religious institutions and denunciations of the Dalai Lama had deepened resentment rather than resolved it.

British officials have in the past raised concerns about human rights in Tibet while also recognizing Tibet as part of the People’s Republic of China. Campaigners, however, said governments had too often allowed economic ties with Beijing to take precedence over human rights.

As protesters dispersed, organizers said the 50th anniversary was both a memorial for those killed in 1959 and 2008 and a renewed appeal for international action. Beijing, meanwhile, continued to insist that Tibet is stable, prosperous and firmly under Chinese sovereignty — and that any challenge to that sovereignty will be met with strong opposition.
